opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to a simple observation: the world we're trying to film is three-dimensional, and the camera is just a projection device. We actually know the physics of that projection extremely well. Perspective projection, pinhole camera models, how parallax works when you move: this is textbook stuff, it's been understood for centuries. So if you ask a purely 2D video model to learn all of that from pixels alone, you're essentially asking it to rediscover projective geometry from scratch, through billions of examples, and it still might get it subtly wrong.

And you see that in practice. When you generate a long video with a lot of camera motion, objects drift, they change shape, a building on the left has a different number of windows when you come back to it. That's because the model doesn't have a persistent notion of "there is a thing out there in space." It only has a notion of "these pixels tend to follow those pixels."

If instead you have an explicit 3D representation, whether that's something like Gaussians, a voxel grid, or some neural field, and you hard-code the camera projection, then a lot of consistency comes for free. The object exists once in the scene, and every frame is just a rendering of it from a different viewpoint. Multi-view consistency isn't something the network has to hope for; it's guaranteed by construction. That's what a good inductive bias does: it removes a whole class of errors so the learning capacity can go toward the parts that are actually hard, like appearance, dynamics, and semantics.

This connects to something I care a lot about from my work on differentiable physics and Taichi. My general philosophy is: whatever you know for sure, build it in; whatever you don't know, learn it. Physics simulators and renderers encode decades of human knowledge. Throwing that away and learning everything end to end is elegant in a way, but it's very data-hungry and it's hard to control. With a 3D representation you also get controllability. You can move the camera exactly where you want, you can edit the scene, you can plug it into a simulator. That's really hard with a black-box 2D generator.

Of course, there are trade-offs. 3D representations are harder to scale, the data is scarcer, and things like fluids, smoke, or reflections can be awkward to represent. So I don't think it's 3D versus 2D forever. I think the most promising direction is a hybrid, where the structure we're confident about, geometry and projection, is explicit, and the messy stuff is handled by learned components. But the camera is about the most certain thing we have, so it seems a bit wasteful not to hard-code it.

r001.rationale: It says hard-coding projection avoids relearning projective geometry and frees learning capacity, but does not state that it saves model parameters.

r002.rationale: It says the object exists once in the scene and is rendered from different viewpoints, guaranteeing multi-view consistency; this communicates that its identity persists as the camera moves around it.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The short answer is that the physical world is three-dimensional, and video is just a two-dimensional measurement of it. A camera with a known projection model is how that measurement actually happens. So when you build a generator that maintains an explicit 3D state and renders it through a fixed, differentiable projection, you are not inventing a constraint. You are writing down something that is true about every real video ever recorded.

Why does that matter for learning? Because a purely 2D model has to discover a huge amount of structure from pixels alone. It has to learn that when the camera pans, everything shifts coherently. That occluded objects persist and come back. That a cup on a table does not change size because you moved the viewpoint. These are regularities a 2D network can approximate given enough data, but it tends to approximate them loosely, and the failures are the ones everyone notices: objects melting, geometry drifting over a few seconds, limbs that stop being attached. If the representation is 3D and the projection is hard-coded, multi-view consistency and temporal consistency are not things you hope the model learns. They fall out of the rendering step for free. The network's capacity goes toward appearance, dynamics, and semantics instead of relearning projective geometry.

The second reason is controllability. In 2D latent space, "move the camera a bit to the left" is a fuzzy semantic instruction. In a 3D representation it is a matrix multiply. Camera trajectory, object placement, lighting, even physics become explicit knobs, which is what you actually want if you are building tools for creators or for simulation rather than just producing impressive clips.

And the third reason comes from my background in simulation and graphics. The graphics community spent decades building rendering pipelines that are correct, fast, and differentiable. Throwing all of that away and asking a transformer to rediscover it is wasteful. Compute is not free, data is not free, and the pixel-only approach has to absorb all of those physical facts from samples. The right place to spend learned capacity is where we genuinely do not have good models: how materials look, how people move, what a plausible scene contains. The right place to use hard-coded structure is where we already know the answer. Projection is firmly in that second category.

The honest caveat is that hard-coding anything introduces a mismatch risk. Real footage has lens distortion, rolling shutter, motion blur, editing cuts. If your projection model is too rigid, the model fights the data. So in practice you want the camera to be a strong prior rather than a straitjacket, with enough learned components to absorb the ways real cameras are messy. But as a default inductive bias, I would rather start from geometry that is correct and let the network handle the residual, than start from nothing and hope.

r001.rationale: The response says hard-coded projection means the model does not have to relearn projective geometry, freeing its capacity for other aspects of video generation.

r002.rationale: It discusses camera motion and multi-view consistency, but does not state that the depicted world retains its identity through a full 360-degree camera rotation.

astra-6.text:
I think the main reason is that a lot of variation in video comes from looking at the same world from different viewpoints. If you generate everything directly in image space, the model has to learn both what the world looks like and how that world changes on the screen when the camera moves. But camera projection is something we already know how to describe mathematically.

So if we use a 3D representation and hard-code the projection, we give the model a useful structure: objects exist in a shared space, and different frames are observations of that space. That helps with consistency. When the camera moves, an object should stay in the same place in the world, and its apparent size and position should change according to the camera geometry. The model doesn't have to rediscover all of that from data.

It also gives us a more direct way to control the camera. Of course, it doesn't solve everything—you still need to model motion, appearance, lighting, and things becoming visible or hidden. But it lets us spend the model's capacity on those harder, less explicitly understood parts, while using known geometry for the projection.

r001.rationale: The response says the model does not have to learn or rediscover camera projection from data and can spend its capacity on harder parts, communicating that hard-coding projection frees model capacity.

r002.rationale: The response discusses consistency as the camera moves, but does not state that the world’s identity is preserved through a complete 360-degree rotation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it helps because a lot of what changes in a video comes from a fairly simple underlying process: you have a 3D world, things move in that world, and a camera projects it into images. If you generate everything directly in pixel space, the model has to learn all of those rules implicitly from data.

With an explicit 3D representation and a fixed projection rule, you give the model some of that structure for free. When the camera moves, perspective, depth, and occlusion can follow from the representation instead of being reinvented frame by frame. That makes it easier to keep objects consistent over time and to control camera motion separately from what’s happening in the scene.

Of course, 3D doesn’t solve everything. You still need to model motion, appearance, and all the complicated things that happen in the world. But camera projection is something we already understand well. Encoding it lets the model spend more of its capacity learning the parts we don’t know how to specify.

r001.rationale: The response says hard-coded projection gives the model structure for free and lets it spend capacity elsewhere, but it does not clearly state that this saves parameters the model would otherwise use to learn projection.

r002.rationale: The response mentions consistency over time and camera motion, but does not state that the depicted world’s identity is preserved through a 360-degree camera rotation.
